nodes.procedure: A dual-electrode AEMWE system was assembled by integrating d-NiOOH/NDL as the anode with a commercial Pt/C cathode. nodes.description: OER performance in 1.0 M KOH using three-electrode configuration
nodes.source_text: Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) analysis revealed the superior OER activity of d-NiOOH, delivering current densities of 100 mAcm⁻² at low overpotentials (201 mV). Tafel slope measurements revealed that d-NiOOH achieved a smaller Tafel slope (46.3 mVdec⁻¹). Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) confirmed the enhanced charge transfer capability of d-NiOOH, showing a substantially lower charge transfer resistance (Rct = 21.0Ω).

nodes.description: OER performance in 1.0 M KOH using three-electrode configuration
nodes.source_text: Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) analysis revealed the superior OER activity of d-NiOOH, outperforming crystalline o-NiOOH (286 mV). Tafel slope measurements revealed that o-NiOOH achieved a larger Tafel slope (110.8 mVdec⁻¹). Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) showed a higher charge transfer resistance (28.2Ω) for o-NiOOH.

nodes.description: OER performance in 1.0 M KOH using three-electrode configuration
nodes.source_text: Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) analysis revealed the superior OER activity of d-NiOOH, surpassing the commercial benchmark catalyst RuO₂ (493 mV). Tafel slope measurements revealed that RuO₂ achieved a Tafel slope of 232.8 mVdec⁻¹.

nodes.description: Stability testing via chronoamperometry at 50 mA/cm² in 1.0 M KOH
nodes.source_text: The electrochemical stability of d-NiOOH was evaluated by the chronoamperometry test. The catalyst operated stably for 300 h at a current density of 50 mAcm⁻² with negligible decay in current density, confirming its exceptional long-term stability for OER.

nodes.description: Differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS) with ¹⁸O-labeled water in 1.0 M KOH
nodes.source_text: Figure 3c,d revealed that ¹⁸O-labeled d-NiOOH exhibited distinct signals at m/z = 32 and 34 (corresponding to ³²O₂ and ³⁴O₂ products, respectively), with the ³⁴O₂ signal intensity markedly exceeding that of ³²O₂. The ³⁴O₂/³²O₂ ratio of d-NiOOH (49.05%) significantly surpassed that of o-NiOOH (18.57%), demonstrating that the disordered structure induces greater activity via LOM during OER.

nodes.description: AEMWE overall water splitting performance at 80°C in 1.0 M KOH
nodes.source_text: Under simulated industrial operating conditions (80°C, 1 M KOH electrolyte), the d-NiOOH/NDL // Pt/C electrolyzer exhibited remarkable overall water splitting performance. The system achieved an industrial-grade current density of 1 Acm⁻² at just 1.79 V. nodes.characterization_summary: Cyclic voltammetry tests showed both a-NiMoO and hc-NiMoO displayed an obvious oxidation peak at 1.2-1.4 V vs RHE. a-NiMoO displayed a more significant oxidation peak and lower peak position potential (1.26 vs 1.31 V vs RHE), indicating the amorphous structure boosted electrochemical reconstruction.
nodes.evidence_snippet: both a-NiMoO and hc-NiMoO displayed an obvious oxidation peak at a potential range of 1.2-1.4 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (vs RHE), indicating the presence of electrochemical reconstruction for generating NiOOH. Furthermore, compared with hc-NiMoO, a-NiMoO displayed a more significant oxidation peak and a lower peak position potential (1.26 vs 1.31 V vs RHE), indicating that the amorphous structure of a-NiMoO could boost the electrochemical reconstruction.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Raman spectroscopy monitored real-time structural evolution during OER. At OCP, Raman bands were observed at 350, 815-900, and 939 cm⁻¹ corresponding to Mo-O vibrations. Upon OER potentials, these bands weakened and disappeared, while new bands appeared at 474 and 557 cm⁻¹ for Ni³⁺-O vibrations in NiOOH. a-NiMoO required 1.4 V vs RHE while hc-NiMoO required 1.6 V vs RHE for reconstruction. The δ(Ni-O)/ν(Ni-O)/O ratio was larger for d-NiOOH than o-NiOOH, indicating higher disorder degree.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Operando Raman spectroscopy was then employed to monitor real-time structural evolution of the catalysts during the OER ... At the open circuit potential (OCP), the Raman bands were observed at 350, 815–900, and 939 cm⁻¹ on the two samples, corresponding to ν₄, ν₃, and ν₁ of Mo–O vibrations ... Upon application of the OER potentials from 1.2 to 1.4 V versus RHE, these Raman bands of a-NiMoO gradually weakened and eventually disappeared at 1.4 V versus RHE. Meanwhile, two new Raman bands appeared at 474 and 557 cm⁻¹ for the δ(Ni³⁻O) bending vibration and ν(Ni³⁻O) stretching vibration modes of NiOOH.

nodes.characterization_summary: X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy revealed pristine a-NiMoO exhibited exclusive Ni²⁺ signatures at 853.9 and 871.5 eV. After reconstruction, peaks shifted to higher binding energies by 0.65 eV, confirming generation of NiOOH. hc-NiMoO retained mixed Ni²⁺/Ni³⁺ oxidation state. Mo 3d spectra showed complete Mo⁶⁺ leaching from a-NiMoO surface (97.5% leaching rate) versus partial leaching from hc-NiMoO (33.4% leaching rate). O 1s spectra revealed d-NiOOH had 37.9% oxygen vacancies versus 25.8% for o-NiOOH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The pristine a-NiMoO exhibited exclusive Ni²⁺ signatures at 853.9 (2p₃/₂) and 871.5 eV (2p₁/₂). After the reconstruction, these two peaks shifted to higher binding energies with a value of 0.65 eV, further confirming the reconstruction to generate NiOOH ... XPS spectra of Mo 3d revealed complete Mo⁶⁺ leaching from the a-NiMoO surface during the reconstruction ... while a small amount of Mo⁶⁺ was preserved on hc-NiMoO ... XPS spectra of O 1s revealed that the content of O-vacancies (Oᵥ) for d-NiOOH catalyst (37.9%) after OER was larger than that for o-NiOOH (25.8%).

nodes.characterization_summary: Electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy showed both d-NiOOH and o-NiOOH displayed an EPR signal with g value of 2.003 corresponding to oxygen vacancies. The intensity of this signal was significantly higher on d-NiOOH, suggesting higher content of oxygen vacancies on d-NiOOH, consistent with XPS results.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Both d-NiOOH and o-NiOOH displayed an EPR signal with a g value of 2.003 corresponding to Oᵥ. Compared with that on o-NiOOH, the intensity of this signal is significantly higher on d-NiOOH, suggesting a higher content of Oᵥ on d-NiOOH, consistent with the results of O 1s XPS spectra.

nodes.characterization_summary: X-ray absorption near edge structure analysis of nickel revealed pristine a-NiMoO exhibited characteristic absorption edge energy of 8342.9 eV matching the +2 oxidation state of NiO. d-NiOOH displayed a 1.5 eV positive edge shift corresponding to an average oxidation state of +3.1. o-NiOOH showed a minor shift after reconstruction from 8342.32 to 8342.7 eV.
nodes.evidence_snippet: X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) analysis of nickel (Figure 2g,h) revealed distinct oxidation pathways: the pristine a-NiMoO exhibited characteristic absorption edge energy (8342.9 eV) matching the +2 oxidation state of NiO, whereas d-NiOOH displayed a 1.5 eV positive edge shift corresponding to an average oxidation state of +3.1.

nodes.characterization_summary: Fourier-transform extended X-ray absorption fine structure spectra exhibited two distinct peaks at 1.6 and 2.6 Å corresponding to Ni-O and Ni-Ni bonds in γ-NiOOH. d-NiOOH showed shortened Ni-O bond lengths compared to o-NiOOH, indicating enhanced Ni-O covalency. EXAFS fitting analysis showed d-NiOOH had Debye-Waller factor of 0.0078 Ų and Ni-O coordination number of 4.9, while o-NiOOH had 0.0063 Ų and 5.6, confirming higher disorder degree of d-NiOOH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: the corresponding Ni K-edge Fourier-transform extended X-ray absorption fine structure (FT-EXAFS) spectra exhibited two distinct peaks at 1.6 and 2.6 Å (Figure 2i), corresponding to the Ni-O and Ni-Ni bonds in γ-NiOOH. Notably, d-NiOOH showed shortened Ni-O bond lengths compared to o-NiOOH, indicating the enhanced Ni-O covalency on d-NiOOH.

nodes.characterization_summary: Positron annihilation spectroscopy revealed three characteristic lifetimes τ1, τ2, and τ3. d-NiOOH exhibited longer τ1 (187 ps) than o-NiOOH (156 ps), suggesting the presence of Mo vacancies in d-NiOOH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: positron annihilation spectroscopy (PAS) was performed. Corresponding PAS results and derived lifetime parameters were shown in Figure S15 and Table S4 (Supporting Information), manifesting three characteristic lifetimes of τ1, τ2, and τ3 ... Crucially, d-NiOOH exhibits a longer τ1 (187 ps) than o-NiOOH (156 ps), suggesting the presence of Mo vacancies in d-NiOOH.

nodes.characterization_summary: Linear sweep voltammetry analysis revealed d-NiOOH delivered current densities of 100 mA/cm² at low overpotential of 201 mV, outperforming o-NiOOH (286 mV) and commercial RuO₂ (493 mV). Carbon paper exhibited negligible OER activity.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) analysis revealed the superior OER activity of d-NiOOH, delivering current densities of 100 mAcm⁻² at low overpotentials (201 mV) (Figure 3a; Figure S23, Supporting Information), outperforming crystalline o-NiOOH (286 mV) and surpassing the commercial benchmark catalyst RuO₂ (493 mV).

nodes.characterization_summary: Tafel slope measurements revealed d-NiOOH achieved a smaller Tafel slope of 46.3 mV/dec compared to o-NiOOH (110.8 mV/dec) and RuO₂ (232.8 mV/dec), demonstrating superior reaction kinetics of d-NiOOH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Tafel slope measurements revealed that d-NiOOH achieved a smaller Tafel slope (46.3 mVdec⁻¹) than o-NiOOH (110.8 mV dec⁻¹) and RuO₂ (232.8 mVdec⁻¹) (Figure 3b), demonstrating the superior reaction kinetics of d-NiOOH.

nodes.characterization_summary: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy confirmed enhanced charge transfer capability of d-NiOOH, showing substantially lower charge transfer resistance (Rct = 21.0 Ω) than o-NiOOH (28.2 Ω).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) confirmed the enhanced charge transfer capability of d-NiOOH, showing a substantially lower charge transfer resistance (Rct = 21.0 Ω) than o-NiOOH (28.2 Ω).

nodes.characterization_summary: Electrochemically active surface area normalization of LSV curves showed the activity trend remained unchanged, indicating d-NiOOH possessed higher intrinsic OER activity. Double-layer capacitance (Cdl) values were 2.2 mF/cm² for d-NiOOH and 2.12 mF/cm² for d-NiOOH-300h.
nodes.evidence_snippet: To compare the intrinsic OER activity of catalysts, we normalized the LSV curves using electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) values (Figure S26, Supporting Information). After ECSA normalization, the activity trend remained unchanged, indicating that d-NiOOH possessed higher intrinsic OER activity.

nodes.characterization_summary: Turnover frequency values at 250 mV overpotential were 0.181 s⁻¹ for d-NiOOH and 0.028 s⁻¹ for o-NiOOH, confirming best intrinsic activity of d-NiOOH for electrocatalytic OER.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The turnover frequency (TOF) values of the above samples were also calculated to reveal their intrinsic activities (Table S5, Supporting Information). At an overpotential of 250 mV, the TOF values of d-NiOOH and o-NiOOH are 0.181 and 0.028 s⁻¹, which confirms the best intrinsic activity of d-NiOOH for electrocatalytic OER.

nodes.characterization_summary: Chronoamperometry test showed d-NiOOH operated stably for 300 h at current density of 50 mA/cm² with negligible decay in current density, confirming exceptional long-term stability for OER.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The electrochemical stability of d-NiOOH was evaluated by the chronoamperometry test. As shown in Figure S28 (Supporting Information), the catalyst operated stably for 300 h at a current density of 50 mAcm⁻² with negligible decay in current density, confirming its exceptional long-term stability for OER.

nodes.characterization_summary: Transmission electron microscopy images of d-NiOOH-300h revealed well-preserved morphology of the flaky amorphous structure after 300 h durability test.
nodes.evidence_snippet: TEM images revealed a well-preserved morphology of the flaky amorphous structure (Figure S29, Supporting Information).

nodes.characterization_summary: Differential electrochemical mass spectrometry measurements with ¹⁸O-labeled d-NiOOH exhibited distinct signals at m/z = 32 and 34 (corresponding to ³²O₂ and ³⁴O₂ products). The ³⁴O₂/³²O₂ ratio of d-NiOOH (49.05%) significantly surpassed that of o-NiOOH (18.57%), demonstrating disordered structure induces greater activity via lattice oxygen-mediated mechanism. Negligible ³⁶O₂ signals (< 0.5%) exclude adjacent oxygen coupling pathways.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 3c,d revealed that ¹⁸O-labeled d-NiOOH exhibited distinct signals at m/z = 32 and 34 (corresponding to ³²O₂ and ³⁴O₂ products, respectively), with the ³⁴O₂ signal intensity markedly exceeding that of ³²O₂, providing preliminary confirmation of LOM dominance in d-NiOOH. In contrast, o-NiOOH showed a predominant ³²O₂ signal with minor ³⁴O₂ signals. Notably, the ³⁴O₂/³²O₂ ratio of d-NiOOH (49.05%) significantly surpassed that of o-NiOOH (18.57%).

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy monitored reaction intermediates during OER. A distinct characteristic peak of the O-O* intermediate was observed at 1122 cm⁻¹ corresponding to superoxo O-O* species prior to O₂ release. The peak intensity of O-O* in d-NiOOH was significantly higher than in o-NiOOH, indicating d-NiOOH generated more O-O* intermediates under same testing conditions, providing evidence for lattice oxygen-mediated mechanism.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Operando FT-IR was further employed to monitor reaction intermediates during OER. As shown in Figure 3e,f, a distinct characteristic peak of the O-O* intermediate was observed at 1122 cm⁻¹, corresponding to the superoxo O-O* species prior to O₂ release. Notably, the peak intensity of O-O* in d-NiOOH was significantly higher than that in o-NiOOH, indicating that d-NiOOH could generate more O-O* intermediates under the same testing conditions.

nodes.characterization_summary: Linear sweep voltammetry measurements across different pH values showed d-NiOOH exhibited significant pH sensitivity with pronounced decrease in OER activity as electrolyte pH decreased. o-NiOOH demonstrated markedly attenuated pH-dependent activity variations, confirming d-NiOOH triggers uncoordinated proton-electron transfer process characteristic of lattice oxygen-mediated mechanism.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As demonstrated by LSV measurements (Figure S34, Supporting Information), the d-NiOOH exhibited significant pH sensitivity, with its OER activity showing a pronounced decrease as the electrolyte pH decreased. In striking contrast, o-NiOOH demonstrated markedly attenuated pH-dependent activity variations across the entire tested range compared to its amorphous counterpart. This disparity unambiguously confirmed that d-NiOOH may trigger the uncoordinated proton-electron transfer process characteristic of the LOM mechanism.

nodes.characterization_summary: Density functional theory calculations showed total density of states near Fermi level significantly increased for d-NiOOH compared to o-NiOOH, indicating structural disorder enhances charge transfer capability and electronic conductivity. Partial density of states analysis revealed disorder induced pronounced shift of Ni 3d and O 2p band centers toward Fermi level, facilitating electron transfer and enhancing metal-oxygen covalency. Rate-determining steps for d-NiOOH showed LOM pathway (1.75 eV) preferred over AEM (2.59 eV), while o-NiOOH showed reversed trend with AEM (1.96 eV) preferred over LOM (2.68 eV).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The total density of states (TDOS) calculation showed a significant increase in total density of states near the Fermi level for d-NiOOH compared to o-NiOOH, indicating that structural disorder effectively enhances charge transfer capability and electronic conductivity ... For d-NiOOH, the rate-determining steps (RDS) for the AEM and LOM correspond to ... with activation barriers of 2.59 and 1.75 eV. This indicated a preferential LOM pathway over AEM in d-NiOOH.
